Appendix G. Synthetic Aviation Fuel Increasing global use of synthetic aviation fuel (SAF) (also known as sustainable aviation fuel) could lead to higher fuel costs for the U.S. Department of War (DOW) and could pose supply chain shortfalls if SAF becomes required for DOW. SAF, after blending with petroleum diesel, is identical to conventional petroleum diesel, as ensured by the international standard ASTM qualification process. SAF functions as a drop-in replacement fuel for blending with conventional jet fuel (Jet A or Jet A1 kerosene) (IATA n.d.) and can be produced from nonpetroleum-based biomass feedstocks (e.g., waste fats, oils, and greases, as well as agricultural and woody biomass and waste) using multiple processes (AFDC n.d.). Although multiple production feedstocks and methods have been approved to meet international standards (Rosales Calderon 2024a), only one is currently commercialized (Rosales Calderon 2024b). With the exception of some older or experimental aircraft and engines not designed to run on conventional jet fuels, adherence to international standards ensures that SAF blends are compatible with existing aircraft engines and fueling equipment. International standard ASTM D7566 defines the technical requirements for SAF, including the eligible feedstocks and pathways to produce SAF (ASTM 2022b), and includes the requirements of ASTM D1655 for conventional jet fuels (ASTM 2022a). When SAF is blended with conventional jet fuel, SAF must meet a list of requirements in D7566 which are designed to guarantee that SAF is identical to the conventional jet fuels which meet D1655 petroleum jet fuel standards. SAF blends meeting these requirements are released to the fungible fuel distribution system as jet fuel, with no designation that it contains a SAF component. This is the case whether it is Jet A, Jet A-1, JP- 8, or JP-5. Because of these standards, different types of SAF must undergo costly and complex certification to ensure safety, performance, and compliance with technical standards and airworthiness requirements, as well as maintain manufacturer warranties. Aircraft and engine manufacturers, the regulatory authorities (e.g., FAA in US and EASA in EU) of the aircraft’s country of registration, and standards organizations (e.g., ASTM international) are all included in the approval process (ASTM 2025). One interviewee expressed concerns that some European military aircraft may not achieve SAF certification in time to keep pace with the civilian sector’s transition to these fuels due to distinct national military certification regimes, the variety of international aircraft/engine origins, and the lack of a strong regulatory mandate equivalent to the EU's civilian targets. Furthermore, some stakeholders have expressed uncertainty regarding SAF performance under conditions (such as high altitudes or rapid maneuvers) that military aircraft may encounter at the extremes of their operating capability which have not yet been fully tested and certified.
